scheduled_change_note.what: Not scheduled by law. DOB, now the lead agency for the construction codes, is reviewing all 12 code categories (Building and Plumbing included) and publishes an estimated timeline only: first notice of proposed rulemaking in fall 2026, second notice in summer 2027, Council review in fall 2027, final codes published in late 2027. No edition or effective date is named.

Public Comment Period (45 Days). Phase 2: Second Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. Early 2027: Prepare content for second notice of proposed rulemaking. Summer 2027: Publish 2nd Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. Public Comment Period (30 Days). Phase 3: Final Codes. Summer 2027: Prepare final codes. Fall 2027: Council Review Period (~80 Days). Late 2027: Publish final codes.

This section sets forth exemptions from permit requirements, subject to historic and flood hazard area restrictions set forth in Sections 105.2.5 and 105.2.6 respectively. Exemptions from permit requirements of the Construction Codes shall not be deemed to grant authorization for any work to be done in any manner in violation of the provisions of the Construction Codes or of any other laws, regulations or ordinances of the District of Columbia. Building: 1. Brick pointing. 2. Caulking, patching and plaster repair of nonrated assemblies. 3. Installation of window screens and storm windows. 4. Repair in kind of existing fences. 5. Application of a paint, sealant, stain or other coating [...] 6. Papering, tiling, carpeting, floor covering, cabinets, countertops and similar finish work. 7. Replacement in kind of one of the items listed hereafter. For the purpose of this section, "replacement in kind" means replacement with a feature of like material that replicates the existing feature in proportion, appearance, texture, design, detail and dimensions. 7.1. Roof covering or coping. 7.2. Siding. 7.3. Gutters and downspouts and fascia. 7.4. Private sidewalks and driveways [...] 7.5. Patios [...] 7.6. Nonrated suspended ceiling tile. 7.7. Not more than 160 square feet (14.9 m2) of gypsum board excluding installation of fire-rated gypsum wall board or shaft liner. 8. A single garden storage shed [...] 9. Prefabricated pools, spas or water features [...] 10. Retaining walls [...] 11. Shade cloth structures [...] 12. Swings and other playground equipment [...] 13. A tree house or playhouse [...] 14. Movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters and partitions not over five feet nine inches (1753 mm) in height. 15. A one-story mausoleum [...] 16. [certain signs] 17. Structures erected for a period of less than 180 days [...] 18. Tents and other membrane structures [...] 19. Erection or replacement of fixed or retractable awnings [...] | 105.2.2 Ordinary repairs. Permits are not required for ordinary repairs to buildings, other structures or equipment. Ordinary repairs shall not include any of the following: 1. The cutting away of any wall, partition or portion thereof, the removal or cutting of any structural beam or load bearing support, or the removal or change of any required means of egress, or rearrangement of parts of a structure affecting the egress requirements. 2. Addition to, alteration of, replacement or relocation of any standpipe, water supply, sewer, drainage, drain leader, gas, soil, waste, vent or similar piping, electric wiring or mechanical or other work affecting public health or general safety.
permit.note: Toilet partitions or compartments are not named. The only 'partitions' in the list are 'movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters and partitions not over five feet nine inches in height' (item 14); the code doesn't say whether a toilet partition anchored to the floor, wall or ceiling counts as movable, and this file doesn't decide it. Item 7's replacement-in-kind list doesn't include partitions. Read in DOB's integrated PDF (Part 1, pages 17 to 19), which doesn't show amendments after May 29, 2020; DOB's current 'How to Get a Permit' page repeats the same list.

other_quotes.quote: What are the sales tax rate(s)? The District of Columbia sales tax rate can vary depending on the service or item subject to sales tax. [...] General Sale or Medical Marijuana - Tax Rate: 6%

Generally, the tax rate on the gross receipts from sales of or charges for tangible personal property and services shall be 6.0%, except for certain enumerated services specified under the DC Code, until September 30, 2027 and then 7.0% beginning October 1, 2027.

contractor.quote: I am a sub-contractor and am only here for one contract. Do I need to get a Basic Business License (BBL)? Yes, you are required to obtain a Basic Business License (BBL) (i.e., General Contractor/Construction Manager, Home Improvement Contractor or Home Improvement Salesperson); the licensure of the contractor for whom you are working is not valid for your contracting business. page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Washington, DC job sites. Price your restroom and see the District's stall counts, permit and license rules.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Washington, DC offices, schools, hotels and museums, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.access_bullet: - **Wheelchair access:** a restroom with stalls needs at least one stall a wheelchair user can enter and use, and a room with six or more stalls and urinals also needs a narrower stall with grab bars on both sides. Federal law and the District's own building rules set the sizes, and the DC Department of Buildings applies them when it reviews permit plans.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** the District's building rules require solid plastic (HDPE) partitions to pass a room-corner fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** the District's building rules set the number of toilets and urinals by how many people use the building. The table below shows what that means.
page.state_extra_bullet: - **District extras:** the District's rules add an 18-inch vertical grab bar beside the toilet in accessible stalls, which the federal rules don't require, and set the narrower stall at 36 inches wide. A restaurant, store or other public venue that needs six or more toilets in total must also have a one-person family restroom.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** in Washington, DC a one-person public restroom must have a gender-neutral sign, such as "Restroom". A building may provide one-person restrooms open to everyone in place of separate men's and women's rooms. Rooms with several stalls are signed for men or women, and the District's building rules don't describe a shared all-gender room with stalls, so ask the DC Department of Buildings before planning one.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** the DC Department of Buildings requires a permit for interior alterations. Its list of work that needs no permit covers tiling, carpeting, cabinets, countertops and similar finish work, and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches. It doesn't name toilet partitions. Ask the Department of Buildings whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.stalls_intro: Washington, DC counts toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. It isn't the number of staff or of visitors in a day. Half are counted as men and half as women. Every toilet needs a stall, and every urinal needs a screen on each side. Urinals are optional: in a men's room they may replace up to half of the toilets in an office and up to two thirds in a restaurant or school, so the table shows the men's side as stalls.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, the District's building rules count an office at one person per 100 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20.
page.install_rule: A contractor working in Washington, DC needs a DC Basic Business License in a contractor category, such as General Contractor/Construction Manager, with liability insurance on file. A subcontractor in the District for a single job needs one too. It is a business license, not a trade exam, so ask the Business Licensing Division of the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection which category fits partition installation. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor working in Washington, DC needs a DC Basic Business License in a contractor category.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on District government construction contracts over $2,000, schools and city buildings included, federal law requires at least the wage the U.S. Department of Labor sets for Washington, DC. For a carpenter on building work that is $34.41 an hour plus $14.33 in benefits.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 6% in Washington, DC. The District has one rate, with no county or city tax on top. The rate is set to rise to 7% on October 1, 2027.
page.tax_install_bullet: - **Tax on installation:** in Washington, DC, installation labor is left out of the taxed price when it is listed separately on the invoice. Minor repair and maintenance work on a building is taxed as a service, but work done as part of construction or major repairs is not. A contractor who supplies materials that become part of the building pays the tax when buying them.
page.buyers_extra: - **Hotels, museums and universities:** finishes that match the building in visitor restrooms, HDPE or phenolic where crowds are hard on stalls.

notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether replacing or adding anchored toilet partitions in an existing commercial restroom needs a DOB permit, and whether DOB treats them as 'movable partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches' (DC Department of Buildings, (202) 671-3500).

The permit list was read in DOB's integrated PDF, which doesn't show amendments after May 29, 2020; DOB's current 'How to Get a Permit' page repeats the same list. Read 12-A DCMR 105.2 on dcregs.dc.gov in a browser.

In historic districts DOB's page says the no-permit list doesn't apply as written; the code limits that to listed exterior items. The page text leaves this out: check with DOB for a building in a historic district.

DOB is rewriting the construction codes and estimates final codes in late 2027 (first proposed rules due fall 2026). Nothing is adopted, so the page doesn't mention it: recheck every figure when the new codes are published.
Sales tax rises to 7% on October 1, 2027 (D.C. Code 47-2002(a)); the date was already moved once from October 1, 2026, so recheck in summer 2027 and update the bullet.

DLCP doesn't say which Basic Business License category covers a commercial partition installer or what the General Contractor classes A, B, C, G and H mean: ask the Business Licensing Division, (202) 671-4500.
Federal buildings in Washington follow federal standards, not the District's codes, and federal contracts carry their own wage rules: not researched, so the page doesn't say it.
The carpenter rate in determination DC20260002 is dated May 1, 2024: check sam.gov for a newer modification before launch.
